text: Greene and Cornwallis faced serious challenges during operations across the topographically diverse area of operations—bounded by the Appalachian Mountains in the west and running about 330 miles from southern Virginia to Savannah, Georgia. Camden and Cheraw were located along the East Coast’s fall line—the highest navigable point on rivers flowing from the mountains to the Atlantic Ocean—and within the Sandhills region, a strip of broad pine barrens cut with flat ridges, stretching from Georgia to North Carolina. Savannah and Charleston were in the lower coastal plain, a mix of gently sloping terrain and wide tidal rivers bordered by marshy, fertile lowlands. In between was the upper coastal plain, with its slightly to steeply sloped clay and gravel ridges covered with thick vegetation. The Battles of Cowpens, South Carolina, and Guilford Courthouse, North Carolina, took place within this geological region. Weather and climate within the Carolina subtropical region were equally diverse. Average summertime high temperatures ranged from 95°F (35°C) in the coastal plains to 75°F (24°C) in the upper parts of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Summertime heat and humidity affected both sides but caused greater hardships for northern European soldiers who were unused to the American climate. Winter daytime highs in the upper coastal plains ranged from 52°F (11°C) to 47°F (8°C), with nighttime lows around 32°F (8°C). The highest amounts of precipitation, mostly rain except in the upper mountain elevations, occurred along the coastal plains. The lower coastal plain averaged 51 to 60 inches (130 to 152 centimeters) of rain annually, and the upper coastal plain received around 46 to 50 inches (117 to 127 centimeters) per year. Heavy rainfall, especially during the peak months of March and July, hindered the cross-country movement of

troops and supply wagons by turning roads into mud and making normally shallow creeks and rivers impassable. Diseases like smallpox and ague (malaria) significantly affected the operations of both armies. Smallpox was endemic in eighteenth-century Europe; thus, most British troops had acquired immunity to it either from inoculation or natural exposure. By contrast, the smaller, largely rural American population was vulnerable to smallpox. Continental and militia forces at Boston and Québec in 1775 were afflicted greatly by smallpox, likely brought over by British troops. Washington subsequently ordered the inoculation of Continental soldiers, which reduced the impact of the smallpox to more manageable levels. Washington also attempted to further reduce camp fevers like typhoid by imposing strict hygiene measures in Continental encampments—practices carried over by Greene’s Continental forces in the South. The pestilent climate of the American South also plagued soldiers, as epidemics of fever derailed American offensives on British East Florida in 1776 and 1778. Clinton was acutely aware of the dangers posed by low country diseases to unacclimated Europeans and timed his 1780 attack on Charleston to take place in winter, when the risks of these illnesses were lower. The protracted American defense of the city, however, frustrated Clinton’s efforts to protect his forces. Many British and German troops fell ill from malaria, and the filth that accumulated during the siege triggered a typhoid outbreak. The movement of British troops and freed Black slaves into the interior caused smallpox outbreaks that lingered in rural areas after the end of the war. Cornwallis’s army was affected greatly by malaria, despite his efforts to avoid the disease by marching his army into the supposedly healthier up-country region. Many soldiers were permanently incapacitated, and several died from fevers. Malaria was no respecter of people, and during October 1780 both Cornwallis and Tarleton temporarily were incapacitated by ague. The northern Continental troops were equally susceptible to malaria, but their surgeons usually carried cinchona bark (also known as Jesuit’s bark) supplied from Spanish-held New Orleans. Cinchona bark contains quinine, a substance known to suppress malarial symptoms. British
surgeons were aware of the bark’s medicinal properties but seldom received enough to make a difference.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
title: The War in the Carolinas and Georgia
